newsitem.title: CHINA: HK stocks to mark new era under China with gains.
newsitem.headline: HK stocks to mark new era under China with gains.

text.p: A new era under China is expected to begin on a firm note for Hong Kong stocks on Thursday, although plans by the new government to increase housing may hurt the property sector.

"There are expectations that the market will rally and that Chinese money will enter the market so that it will close higher under the new flag," said Franklin Lam, director of research at SBC Warburg. "The non-property segment will do very well."
After winding up its final trading day under British rule last Friday at a record closing high, the market took a three-day holiday to celebrate Hong Kong's return to China at midnight on Monday.

The blue chip Hang Seng Index rose 68.77 points, or 0.45 percent, to 15,196.79 on Friday. The red chip Hang Seng China-Affiliated Corporations Index surged 224.63 points, or 6.92 percent, to 3,469.32.

"It (the return to China) is a significant event for the Chinese -- it is a sentiment thing," said Kent Rossiter, institutional sales manager at Nikko Securities. "The handover is a celebration of being Chinese and there will be a lot of interest in the red chips," he said.

"Except for the change in the flag, there is not much change at all," said Alex Tang, head of research at Yamaichi International. "We are focusing on two things -- one is the government housing policy and the other is the direction of interest rates."

Hong Kong chief executive Tung Chee-hwa said in his inaugural speech on Tuesday that his administration would take action to curb high property prices and would increase the number of overall housing units to at least 85,000 a year.
"What this amounts to is that the government will be providing a consistent supply of housing. Tung will not be making friends with the (property) developers," said Lam.
"I think developer stocks will be soft at the opening."

While the market waits for specific details on how the government plans to curb property speculation and implement its housing policy, property stocks were likely to suffer from the uncertainty, analysts said.
Other blue chips could move selectively higher but the focus on Thursday was likely to be on red chip stocks, they said.

"Blue chips are not going to make a big jump but as far as the red chips are concerned, they look like they have the momentum to go higher," said Tang. "We will probably see this kind of divergence in the month to come."

Driven by retail investors and money from mainland China, positive sentiment surrounding Hong Kong's change in sovereignty should lead to heavy trading in red chip stocks -- shares of mainland-controlled Hong Kong-based companies, analysts said.
"They already put on a strong performance on Friday in anticipation of another rally. They will probably go up," said Lam.
A two-day U.S. Federal Reserve policy-setting meeting is likely to end later on Wednesday with steady interest rates, which could buoy the market further, analysts said.
"I still see upside for Hong Kong," said Rossiter, adding that the Hang Seng Index could hit 15,600 to 15,800 points this month.
